joist: Joist is designed for the moment you are standing in front of a customer and need to put a number on the job. You build the estimate on a phone, send it for approval, and convert it into an invoice once the work is done. The AI element is thin — the real value is speed from quote to payment without going back to the office.
togal-ai: Togal.AI reads construction drawings and produces quantities automatically, which is the part of estimating that normally eats entire evenings. You upload plans, it identifies rooms, areas and assemblies, and you adjust rather than measure from scratch. It is aimed squarely at plan-based bidding, so it matters most if you price from drawings rather than from a site visit.
knowify: Knowify is built around a question most software ignores: did that job actually make money? It tracks the estimate against real costs as the job progresses, so overruns show up while you can still react. Change orders and progress billing are handled as first-class features rather than afterthoughts.
contractor-foreman: Contractor Foreman tries to cover everything a small contractor would otherwise spread across spreadsheets — estimating, scheduling, daily logs, documents and costs — at a price point below the enterprise platforms. It is not the most polished tool in any single category, but for a small firm that wants one system instead of five, that trade-off often makes sense.
housecall-pro: In practice Housecall Pro becomes the record for the entire job: the customer books, the technician receives the job on a phone, the invoice is generated on completion, and payment is collected before the van leaves. Its AI features target the tasks that quietly consume office hours — chasing review requests, following up quotes and answering routine questions.
jobber: Jobber is usually the first real system a home service business adopts after paper and spreadsheets. The quoting-to-invoice flow is the strongest part: send a quote, get approval online, convert it to a job, then invoice and collect. Recent AI features assist with scheduling suggestions and customer follow-up rather than replacing the core workflow.
servicetitan: ServiceTitan is what trade businesses move to when they have multiple crews, a dedicated office team and enough volume that dispatch efficiency is worth real money. Its depth is genuine — dispatch, price book, marketing attribution and reporting all live in one place. The cost and the implementation effort are substantial, which is why it suits established operations rather than start-ups.
workiz: Workiz is notable for treating the phone as part of the job system rather than something separate. Calls, texts and job records sit together, so a missed call is visible as a missed opportunity instead of disappearing. It is cheaper and easier to start than the enterprise platforms, at the cost of depth on complex job costing.
fieldedge: FieldEdge has been around long enough to be trade-specific in the details that matter — dispatch boards, price books and accounting integration for HVAC, plumbing and electrical work. The interface is less modern than newer competitors and pricing is not published, which makes evaluation slower, but it remains a serious option for mid-sized firms.
quickbooks: QuickBooks is where most trade businesses end up because their accountant already uses it. Invoicing, expenses, VAT and reporting all work, and almost every other tool integrates with it. What it lacks is job costing — knowing whether an individual job was profitable usually needs an add-on or a separate system alongside it.
freshbooks: FreshBooks is invoicing and basic accounting without the weight of a full accounting suite. For an owner-operator who wants to send professional invoices, track time and get paid online, it is easier to live with than QuickBooks. It is less suited to construction work, where job costing and progress billing matter more than simple invoicing.
xero: Xero is cloud accounting with a large marketplace of add-ons, which is how most trade businesses get job costing — by connecting a specialist tool on top. Unlimited users on many plans is a genuine advantage over per-seat competitors. The trade-off is that the features a contractor needs usually arrive through paid add-ons.
podium: Podium consolidates the customer conversations that otherwise scatter across texts, webchat and social messages into a single inbox, then layers review collection and payments on top. For trades where the first contact is a text rather than a call, that consolidation is the whole point. Pricing is contract-based, so it is worth understanding the exit terms before signing.
smith-ai: Smith.ai exists to solve one expensive problem: the phone ringing while you are under a house or on a roof. An AI receptionist answers, qualifies the enquiry and books the work, escalating to a live agent when the conversation needs judgement. Per-call pricing is unpredictable in busy months, but so is the cost of a missed job.
structurely: Structurely handles the long gap between an enquiry and a decision, which is where remodelling and roofing leads usually die. It follows up by text and email, answers questions and hands the conversation to a human once the lead is qualified. It is deliberately built for considered purchases, not same-day service calls.
tidio: Tidio puts a chat widget on your website that answers routine questions and captures contact details when you are unavailable. The free tier is usable, which makes it a low-risk way to stop losing visitors who will not pick up the phone. The AI needs some tuning, or it will confidently answer questions it should not.
companycam: CompanyCam solves the dispute problem: when a customer questions what was done, timestamped and location-stamped photos end the argument. Crew members take photos on their phones and they land in the correct job automatically, tagged and searchable. The value depends entirely on the crew actually taking the photos, so adoption matters more than features.
raken: Raken replaces the end-of-day paper chase for daily reports. Field staff complete logs on a phone in minutes, and the office gets consistent records for compliance, progress and owner reporting. It is most valuable on longer projects where daily documentation is contractually required, and less relevant to short service jobs.
openspace: OpenSpace turns a walk with a 360 camera into a complete visual record of a site, stitched and navigable afterwards. It means progress can be verified remotely and disputes about what existed at a given date can be settled from the record. Enterprise pricing puts it firmly in the large-project category.
autodesk-construction-cloud: Autodesk Construction Cloud is document and project control for projects with too many drawings, versions and RFIs to manage by email. It integrates with the wider Autodesk ecosystem and scales well. For a small trade business it is heavy and expensive; for a contractor running large projects it is often unavoidable.
birdeye: Birdeye automates the two things that drive local trade work: reviews and listings. It requests reviews after jobs, keeps business details consistent across directories, and uses AI to draft responses. It is contract-priced and not cheap for a one-van operation, but review volume is one of the few marketing levers with a direct local effect.
canva-magic-studio: Canva is how most small trade businesses produce their own marketing material without hiring anyone. The AI features generate images, write draft copy and resize a design for every channel. The risk is generic-looking output — templates are widely recognised if used unmodified, so the branding should be adjusted.
jasper: Jasper is a writing tool aimed at marketing output at volume — ads, landing pages, email sequences and social posts. It maintains brand voice settings, which matters when several people produce content. It only makes financial sense if you publish regularly; occasional users will find general-purpose assistants better value.
semrush: Semrush is the research layer behind local search: what people search for in your area, who currently ranks, and what is technically broken on your site. It is powerful but has a steep learning curve. For a trade business it earns its keep mainly through local keyword tracking and competitor research, not the full feature set.
dext: Dext exists to end the shoebox of receipts. Photograph a receipt and it extracts the supplier, date, amount and category, then pushes a coded entry into your accounting system. The saving shows up at month end and again at year end when your accountant is not reconstructing a year of paper.
expensify: Expensify scans receipts and matches them to card transactions, which suits businesses where staff buy materials on the move. The free tier covers light use. It is worth noting that the pricing model has changed more than once, which has frustrated long-standing users.
chatgpt: ChatGPT is the most flexible tool here and the one most likely to be genuinely useful on a daily basis — drafting quotes and emails, explaining a regulation in plain language, summarising a specification or writing job adverts. Its failure mode is confident invention, so anything technical, legal or regulatory needs checking before it reaches a customer.
claude: Claude's practical advantage is handling long documents: specifications, contracts and tender documents that exceed what other assistants can take in at once. It summarises and answers questions about them accurately enough to be useful for a first pass. It is not a substitute for professional advice on contract terms.
otter-ai: Otter records site meetings and client calls, producing a searchable transcript and a summary afterwards. It is valuable when a conversation covers more than anyone can write down, and when you later need to establish exactly what was agreed. Background noise on site reduces accuracy, so it works best for meetings rather than while work is underway.
grammarly: Grammarly's value for a trade business is unglamorous but real: quotes, emails and proposals that read professionally and contain no typos. It works directly in the browser and in email, so it catches mistakes at the point of writing. The free tier handles spelling and grammar; paid tiers push style suggestions fairly aggressively.
motion: Motion automatically arranges your day around what is actually due, and rearranges it when a job runs long. For an owner-operator moving between estimates, site visits and admin, that removes a constant low-level planning burden. It only works if you commit to keeping your tasks in it rather than in your head.
loom: Loom is for the explanation that would take ten minutes to write and ninety seconds to say — walking a customer through what you found, or showing a team member a detail on site. Recordings come with automatic transcripts and summaries. Some customers still prefer a written summary, so it complements rather than replaces written communication.
